lead: A screen is built from small views, and each basic view has its own input model. A TextView only shows text. An EditText lets the user type. A CheckBox lets the user pick many things; a RadioGroup lets them pick exactly one. Picker views — Spinner, DatePicker, TimePicker, NumberPicker — make the user choose from a fixed set. List views show many rows, and they never store the data themselves: an adapter hands out row views one at a time, only for the rows on screen. This chapter covers those views and the adapter idea behind every list.
prereq: You need: 3.1 Screen components and layouts for views and ViewGroups, and Unit 2 for activities and the onCreate method, because listeners are wired up there.

blocks.text: A TextView displays text and the user cannot edit it. android:textSize="16sp" sets the size in scale-independent pixels: sp follows the user's system font setting, dp does not, so text should use sp. android:textColor="#FF1A237E" is an ARGB colour. android:maxLines="2" with android:ellipsize="end" stops a long string at two lines and ends it with "...".

An EditText is a TextView the user can type into. android:hint shows grey placeholder text while the field is empty; the hint is not a value, and getText().toString() returns an empty string, not the hint. android:inputType chooses which keyboard appears. It does not validate anything: you still read the text and check it yourself.

A Button is a TextView that is clickable by default. Set android:text and attach setOnClickListener. An ImageButton shows a drawable from android:src instead of text, so give it android:contentDescription, otherwise a screen reader announces nothing useful.
A CheckBox has two states and is independent: several check boxes on one screen can be ticked at the same time. Read it with isChecked(), which returns true or false.

A RadioButton also has two states, but it must sit inside a RadioGroup. The group is the part that enforces the rule: ticking one button clears the others in that group. Two RadioGroups on one screen are separate; one button in each can be on. Read the choice with radioGroup.getCheckedRadioButtonId(), which returns the resource id of the ticked button, or -1 when nothing is ticked.
Switch and ToggleButton are on/off controls with the same isChecked() reading. A ToggleButton shows android:textOn and android:textOff; a Switch shows a sliding thumb.
AutoCompleteTextView is an EditText with a drop-down of suggestions from an adapter. setThreshold(1) opens the list after one typed character. The user may still type anything; the list only helps.

A Spinner is a one-line drop-down. Fill it statically with android:entries="@array/plans" from a string array, or in code with spinner.setAdapter(new ArrayAdapter<>(this, android.R.layout.simple_spinner_item, plans)). Listen with setOnItemSelectedListener; the callback is onItemSelected(AdapterView<?> parent, View view, int position, long id).

items: Android calls onItemSelected once while laying the spinner out, with position 0, before the user touches it.
getSelectedItemPosition() returns the index, getSelectedItem() returns the object at that index.
setSelection(3) changes the choice but does not call the listener.

blocks.text: A DatePicker is set with init(year, month, day, listener). The month is 0-based: month 2 means March. getMonth() returns 0 to 11 and getDayOfMonth() returns 1 to 31. A TimePicker gives getHour() (0 to 23 in 24-hour mode, set by setIs24HourView(true)) and getMinute() (0 to 59). A NumberPicker is a wheel of numbers: set setMinValue, setMaxValue, setValue, and read getValue().

A ListView shows a scrolling column of rows and stores no data of its own. The data lives in your list; an adapter is the bridge that turns list entries into row views on demand. The same pattern runs every list-style view in Android.

items: You keep the data in an ordinary list, for example String[] items.
You wrap it: new ArrayAdapter<>(this, android.R.layout.simple_list_item_1, items).
The built-in row layout simple_list_item_1 is one TextView with id android.R.id.text1.
listView.setAdapter(adapter) asks the adapter how many rows exist and calls its getView for each row that becomes visible.

blocks.text: A tap arrives at setOnItemClickListener as onItemClick(AdapterView<?> parent, View view, int position, long id). Here parent is the ListView, view is the row that was tapped, position is the row's index inside the adapter, and id is the row id the adapter reports (for an ArrayAdapter it equals position). getItemAtPosition(position) asks the adapter for the object at that index.

Only the rows on screen exist as views. When a row scrolls off, Android keeps its view and passes it back as convertView to getView(int position, View convertView, ViewGroup parent). Reuse it when it is not null and inflate only when it is null. A small ViewHolder object can cache the child lookups. After changing the backing list, call notifyDataSetChanged(), or the screen keeps the old rows.

figure.caption: Five strings held by one ArrayAdapter, indexed 0 to 4. The tap at index 2 reaches onItemClick as position 2 and returns "Pear"; after setSelection(3) the spinner reports position 3 and its item is "Kiwi".

spec.title: Adapter data and positions
spec.aria: Five strings Fig, Plum, Pear, Kiwi, Lime under indices 0 to 4; index 2 is marked as the tapped row and index 3 as the spinner selection after setSelection(3).

examples.question: A ListView is bound by an ArrayAdapter to five items shown with simple_list_item_1: Fig, Plum, Pear, Kiwi, Lime. The user taps the third row. Give the arguments of onItemClick and say what getItemAtPosition(2) returns. Then the same five entries fill a Spinner whose default selection is index 0; after setSelection(3), what do getSelectedItemPosition() and getSelectedItem() return?
steps: Adapter indices start at 0: Fig = 0, Plum = 1, Pear = 2, Kiwi = 3, Lime = 4.
The third row is index 2, so the callback is onItemClick(parent, view, position, id) with position = 2.
parent is the ListView object, view is the tapped row View, and id is the row id reported by the adapter, which for an ArrayAdapter equals 2.
getItemAtPosition(2) asks the adapter for the object at index 2, which is the string "Pear".
The Spinner starts at index 0, giving "Fig". setSelection(3) moves the choice to index 3, which is "Kiwi".
So getSelectedItemPosition() returns 3 and getSelectedItem() returns "Kiwi".
examples.answer: onItemClick receives position = 2 and getItemAtPosition(2) returns "Pear"; after setSelection(3) the Spinner reports getSelectedItemPosition() = 3 and getSelectedItem() = "Kiwi".
examples.check:
items = ["Fig", "Plum", "Pear", "Kiwi", "Lime"]
position = items.index("Pear")
selected = 3
print(position)
print(selected)
examples.output:
position = 2
getItemAtPosition(2) = Pear
getSelectedItemPosition() = 3
getSelectedItem() = Kiwi

traps: position is the index inside the adapter, so it shifts the moment a header or footer view is added; id is the row id the adapter reports. Treating id as the index taps the wrong row.
Changing the backing list does not redraw the ListView. Without notifyDataSetChanged() the screen keeps the old rows, a favourite one-mark question.
DatePicker months are 0-based: getMonth() returns 0 for January, so the displayed month is getMonth() + 1.

A Spinner fires onItemSelected once during layout with position 0, and setSelection() does not fire it. Code that opens a network call inside the listener runs on screen load even if the user never touches the spinner.
android:inputType only changes the keyboard; it is not validation. A numberPassword field still returns whatever characters the user pastes.

quiz.q: Which attribute sets text size, and which unit should text use?
quiz.a: android:textSize, with sp (scale-independent pixels) so the text grows with the user's font setting.

quiz.q: Why must RadioButtons be placed inside a RadioGroup instead of directly in a LinearLayout?
quiz.a: The RadioGroup is the container that clears the other buttons when one is ticked. RadioButtons loose in a LinearLayout can all stay ticked at once, so single choice is not enforced.

quiz.q: A ListView uses an ArrayAdapter over Fig, Plum, Pear, Kiwi, Lime, and a header view is added at position 0. The user taps Pear. What position does onItemClick receive?
quiz.a: The header takes index 0, so Fig = 1, Plum = 2, Pear = 3. onItemClick receives position = 3, while getItemAtPosition(3) returns "Pear".

quiz.q: A Spinner over the same five entries is created with no explicit setSelection call. What does onItemSelected report during layout, and what does getSelectedItem() return then?
quiz.a: Android calls onItemSelected once with position = 0 and id = 0, so getSelectedItem() returns "Fig". The method is not waiting for a user tap.

quiz.q: Explain why a ListView with 1000 items does not create 1000 row views, and what convertView is for.
quiz.a: Only the rows on screen are inflated, roughly ten. When a row scrolls off, its view is handed back as convertView, so getView inflates only when convertView is null; otherwise it refills the old view with new data. That keeps memory and scrolling cost flat as the list grows.

quiz.q: What is the difference between android:hint and the value of an EditText?
quiz.a: The hint is grey placeholder text shown only while the field is empty. getText().toString() returns an empty string when nothing is typed; it never returns the hint.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real apps ListView is largely replaced by RecyclerView, which forces the ViewHolder pattern and adds DiffUtil for animating changes. Paging libraries feed very long lists a page at a time, and Jetpack Compose swaps adapters for a LazyColumn that takes a data list and a row lambda. Search next for RecyclerView.Adapter, ListAdapter and DiffUtil, then LazyColumn in Compose. Unit 4's CursorAdapter is the database version of the same adapter idea.
